title: Anglicans
hookLine: the Church of England and its worldwide family: a middle way, the Book of Common Prayer

cards: These words turn up at weddings, even for people who never set foot in a church: dearly beloved, we are gathered together here. For better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health.

And at funerals: earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. Those lines, give or take a word, come from one book, shaped above all by one man, an archbishop named Thomas Cranmer, in the 1540s and 50s.
He was later burned at the stake for his faith. His book taught generations to pray in their own language, and quietly shaped English itself. It's called the Book of Common Prayer.
Common, as in shared: the same prayers, said together, by everyone.

teach.h: A WORLDWIDE FAMILY, STRONG IN AFRICA.
teach.b: Anglicans are the Church of England and the worldwide churches that grew from it: the Episcopal Church in the United States, the Church of Nigeria, the Church of Uganda, the Anglican Church of Australia and many more, with large and growing churches in Africa.

The break with Rome came under King Henry the Eighth in the 1530s, tangled up with his marriage and politics as much as faith. But under Cranmer, and later Queen Elizabeth the First, the church found its own shape.

teach.h: CATHOLIC AND REFORMED: A MIDDLE WAY.
teach.b: Anglicans came to call it a middle way: Catholic in its bishops, creeds and sacraments; Reformed in its stress on scripture, grace, and worship in the people's own language.
Some lean toward the Catholic side, with incense and vestments; some toward the evangelical, with preaching and plain services. They share one book of prayer, in many languages.
One small form runs all through it: the collect. That's COL-lect, stress on the first syllable, a short prayer that gathers the people's prayers into one sentence.
It usually names God, remembers something God has done, asks, and ends through Christ.

teach.h: UNTO WHOM ALL HEARTS BE OPEN.
teach.b: Here's one from the start of the 1662 communion service: "Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid: Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts by the inspiration of thy Holy Spirit, that we may perfectly love thee, and worthily magnify thy holy Name; through Christ our Lord. Amen."

teach.h: FROM WHOM NO SECRETS ARE HID.
teach.b: One sentence. That's the Anglican genius: large things said in few, careful words.

how: Anglicans worship from a prayer book, with set prayers, readings and collects for each Sunday; many churches say Morning and Evening Prayer daily and celebrate Holy Communion weekly.

games.q: you're Thomas Cranmer in the 1540s. most of England's worship is in Latin, which most people don't understand. what do you do?
o: keep it in Latin, it's tradition.
write a book of prayer in English for everyone to say together.
let each church make up its own.
games.why: Cranmer wrote the Book of Common Prayer in English, the same prayers for everyone. its words still echo at weddings and funerals.

practice: If you pray, say the Collect for Purity slowly, a phrase per breath: Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid. Stop there, nothing hidden; add the rest if you wish.
If you don't pray, sit with the idea of being fully known, and not turned away.
